title: A Fossil Date Is a Floor

scenes.tts: Rocks about 3.48 billion years old in the Dresser Formation of Western Australia hold layered mounds. A 2017 study read them as traces of life in hot springs. So when did life begin? These rocks cannot say. They tell you that life existed by then. Older traces could have been destroyed, never formed, or not yet found.
scenes.visual: Layered mounds labelled Dresser Formation shrink onto a timeline at 3.48 billion years; a red dashed zone of question marks opens to the older side with three reasons.
scenes.narration: Rocks about 3.48 billion years old in the Dresser Formation of Western Australia hold layered mounds. A 2017 study read them as traces of life in hot springs. So when did life begin? These rocks cannot say. They tell you that life existed by then. Older traces could have been destroyed, never formed, or not yet found.

scenes.tts: Fossils are rarely dated directly. Minerals in the rocks around them are. Take a hypothetical zircon from volcanic ash. It took up uranium as it formed, but almost no lead. Nearly all its lead comes from later decay. So the mineral works like an hourglass. The sand in the bottom bulb tells you the time since it was turned over. The half-life is the time for half the parent atoms to decay. Here, it is 704 million years.
scenes.visual: A crystal holds four orange uranium dots and no lead; an hourglass appears beside it; after one half-life, two dots turn green and become lead while sand falls.
scenes.narration: Fossils are rarely dated directly. Minerals in the rocks around them are. Take a hypothetical zircon from volcanic ash. It took up uranium as it formed, but almost no lead. Nearly all its lead comes from later decay. So the mineral works like an hourglass. The sand in the bottom bulb tells you the time since it was turned over. The half-life is the time for half the parent atoms to decay. Here, it is 704 million years.

scenes.tts: Now suppose the zircon has stayed closed since it formed. You measure three lead atoms for every uranium atom. Every lead atom was once a uranium atom. So the zircon started with four. One quarter is left. That is two half-lives. Two times 704 is 1,408 million years. This is a model, only as good as its assumptions.
scenes.visual: A crystal with one orange and three green dots; the green dots turn back into orange to give four, then the decay is replayed in two half-life steps to one quarter, ending on 1,408 million years.
scenes.narration: Now suppose the zircon has stayed closed since it formed. You measure three lead atoms for every uranium atom. Every lead atom was once a uranium atom. So the zircon started with four. One quarter is left. That is two half-lives. Two times 704 is 1,408 million years. This is a model, only as good as its assumptions.

scenes.tts: Now date a fossil. The ash lies above a fossil bed. A second ash, below the bed, is dated to 1,450 million years. So the fossils are younger than 1,450 and older than 1,408 million years. The answer is a bracket, not a point.
scenes.visual: A rock column with ash on top, a fossil bed, and ash below; dotted lines drop to an age axis where a yellow bracket spans the two dates.
scenes.narration: Now date a fossil. The ash lies above a fossil bed. A second ash, below the bed, is dated to 1,450 million years. So the fossils are younger than 1,450 and older than 1,408 million years. The answer is a bracket, not a point.

scenes.tts: Each fossil first is a minimum age. The oldest fossil sets a floor, and the lineage may be older. Preservation is uneven in space and time, so a gap in the record is not a gap in life. The bias works at the other end too. A species' last fossil usually lies below where it actually vanished.
scenes.visual: One species drawn as a line with sparse fossil dots: a red dashed extension past the oldest dot, a bracketed gap where the line continues, and a red cross to the right of the last dot where it vanished.
scenes.narration: Each fossil first is a minimum age. The oldest fossil sets a floor, and the lineage may be older. Preservation is uneven in space and time, so a gap in the record is not a gap in life. The bias works at the other end too. A species' last fossil usually lies below where it actually vanished.

scenes.tts: So read every date the same way. It has a measured age, a method, an uncertainty, and a direction in which the truth could lie. The Dresser rocks show that life existed by 3.48 billion years ago. The oldest fossil tells you when life existed by, never when it began.
scenes.visual: Four chips for age, method, uncertainty and direction; the Dresser timeline returns with its red zone, ending on the take-home line.
